title: Pagechain Serialization Bottleneck — Case Diary
content:
Executive summary:

This diary documents an investigation into a recurring production regression where end-to-end tail latency spiked for mixed chat workloads. Root cause analysis points to a previously under-observed mode of cache pressure we are calling "pagechain serialization": long, contiguous chains of resident/nonresident page references that force serialized pagewalks and NVMe reads, amplifying memory-bandwidth contention and triggering aggressive eviction cascades. The effect reduces effective reuse and inflates paging throughput, making our KV cache look like it has dramatically lower hit-rate under bursty, mixed-seqlen patterns.

Why this matters:
- 99p request latency increased from ~220ms to ~420ms under a steady 3x traffic spike on Dedicated pools.
- Measured NVMe read bandwidth rose from 6 GB/s baseline to sustained 22–24 GB/s on affected hosts.
- Observed reuse-rate (sampled per-request) dropped from ~78% to ~42% during incidents, but sampled access density suggested the working set hadn't changed that dramatically — indicates serialization rather than pure cache pressure.

How we found it (timeline snippets):
- 2024-10-30: First alert (internal): Dedicated pool dp-west2-7 showed tail-latency alerts during a marketing-driven traffic burst.
- 2024-10-31: SRE triage: spike correlated with higher NVMe saturation but normal GPU utilization.
- 2024-11-03: Instrumented per-page access traces (lightweight sampling) and added additional nvme io latency histogram telemetry.
- 2024-11-07: Confirmed correlated sequences of page faults from samples — many faults are to contiguous logical page ranges that map to the same NVMe stripe and cause serialized IO.
- 2024-11-15–12/04: Lab reproduction and microbenchmarks.
- 2025-01-10: First mitigation deployed (background read-ahead jitter + staggered eviction), lowered incident frequency by ~40%.
- 2025-02-12: Patch PR submitted to allow parallel pagechain walks + admission heuristics (PR #1284).

Key observations and measurements:
- Reuse vs serialization interaction: When a request mix produced long prefix chains (many requests stepping through contiguous KV pages due to similar hot-prompts or shared model prefixes), the page resolver performed sequential pagewalks and NVMe reads. These reads contend on PCIe/NVMe scheduler and block the CPU threads doing the next-stage batching work.
- Bandwidth spike shape: boot-strapped incidents show a steep climb in NVMe throughput followed by intermittent drops corresponding to eviction windows — pattern consistent with streaming reads that starve background writeback and eviction threads, producing thrash.
- CPU vs IO: CPU utilization for inference threads remained moderate; blocker was IO wait and thread stalls waiting on page population. Perf counters show increased instructions-per-pagefault.
- Paging latency: tail of page population latency stretched from median 1.6ms to 12–28ms during incidents depending on NVMe queue depth.

Repro steps (lab):
1) Build a synthetic requester that replays sampled request traces with preserved key-affinity and seqlen distribution from incident traces.
2) Use a host with identical NVMe model and config.
3) Start with warm cache at 80% occupancy, then ramp concurrent sessions to 2.5x baseline producing mixed seqlen (short chat + long-context summaries).
4) Collect: per-page miss traces, nvme iostat (qdepth), per-thread stack traces, and reuse histograms.

Microbenchmarks and tooling used:
- pagewalk-tracer (in-house lightweight tracer) — collects page id streams per request.
- fio with sequential small-block randomization to emulate stripe contention.
- perf + bpftrace snippets to capture stack during page fault wakes.
- nvme-cli iostat and kernel block latency histograms.
- eBPF script to capture average queue depth for NVMe per 10s window.

Experiment matrix and results (short):
- Baseline (no change): reuse 78%, NVMe 6 GB/s, tail lat 220ms.
- Inject contiguous access sequences (synthetic): reuse drops to 46%, NVMe 20–23 GB/s, tail lat 410ms.
- Apply background read-ahead jitter (randomized 2–20ms offsets): incident rate down ~40%, tail lat 320ms.
- Reduce reservation window for prefetch from 5s->1s: lowers sustained NVMe throughput but increases cold-start p99 for some long-context requests by ~10–12%. Tradeoff.
- Parallel pagechain walks prototype (2x threads per chain): reduces page population tail to ~6ms and NVMe queue depth smoothing, reuse recovered to ~67% in lab.

Hypotheses refined during investigation:
- H1: Serialization primarily stems from our page population code walking chains sequentially and issuing synchronous reads per page.
- H2: NVMe scheduler and stripe alignment exacerbate the problem when many requests hit adjacent addresses.
- H3: Long prefetch / reservation windows amplify the problem by holding slots for pages that are late to be used, reducing effective concurrency.

Short-term mitigations (deployed or staged):
- Add small randomized jitter to background read-ahead and prefetch timings (deployed 2025-01-10).
- Reduce prefetch reservation window defaults for Dedicated pools by 3x (staged).
- Circuit-breaker: if per-host NVMe QD > 32 and resident reuse drops > 35% within 30s, switch new requests to fallback model variant with smaller KV footprint (requires routing change).

Medium-term design changes (engineering work):
- Parallel pagechain resolver: allow pagechain population to be parallelized across N worker tasks with coordination to avoid double-populating. Early prototype shows ~35–50% improvement in worst-case page fill tail.
- Pagechain coalescing: detect contiguous page sequences and issue coalesced IO with larger block size for NVMe (fewer IOs, better throughput shape).
- Bank-aware placement: reduce stripe collisions by distributing logical page ids across banks for known hot prefixes (needs experiment with placement algorithm).
- Eviction backoff: adaptive eviction that reduces active churn when NVMe latency rises (treat NVMe queue depth as congestion signal).

Runbook additions (operational):
- New telemetry to add: per-host "pagechain-length-percentiles" (sampled), NVMe queue-depth smoothed 30s, page-population tail histogram.
- Incident run criteria: when reuse-rate drops > 35% and NVMe bandwidth > 18 GB/s for 2 consecutive 1m windows => fire incident.
- Immediate actions on incident: shift traffic to separate pool, enable ingress throttling for non-critical routes, toggle prefetch jitter to on, escalate to eng-serving-runtime.

Open tasks and owners:
- D1 (Diego): Finish parallel resolver prototype, bench on synthetic traces, PR by 2025-02-05. (PR #1284).
- D2 (Ava): Implement pagechain-length telemetry + dashboards, due 2025-01-18.
- D3 (Priya): Run bank-placement experiments on a small fleet and collect eviction vs bandwidth curves, due 2025-01-30.
- D4 (SRE): Add NVMe QD + reuse-rate alert and new incident page template, due 2025-01-12.

Risks and tradeoffs:
- Parallelization reduces tail but increases complexity and risk of race conditions around slot accounting. Need strong invariants and thorough testing under multi-tenant workloads.
- Coalesced IO helps NVMe throughput but may increase read amplification for small-access patterns (wasteful on egress bandwidth).
- Aggressive prefetch reduction reduces NVMe pressure but increases cold-start p99 for long-context customers. Must balance via per-customer SLOs.

Conclusions / recommendations:
- The combination of long contiguous pagechains + sequential population is a realistic and recurring cause of tail latency spikes. It is not a simple eviction tuning problem — it is a serialization/IO-shape problem layered above normal reuse dynamics.
- Short-term mitigations (jitter, reservation window reduction, circuit-breaker routing) are effective at reducing incident frequency and buy engineering time.
- Medium-term investments in parallel page population, coalesced IO, and bank-aware placement look promising and should be prioritized (parallel resolver first).

Appendix: useful commands / traces used during investigation:
- Collect page traces: sudo /opt/infra/bin/pagewalk-tracer --sample 1/100 --out /tmp/trace.pw
- NVMe queue depth histogram (bpf): bpftrace scripts/nvme_qd.bt -o nvme_qd.log
- fio test for stripe contention: fio --name=stripe --ioengine=libaio --bs=4k --size=2G --numjobs=4 --rw=randread

Notes to reviewers:
- This diary mixes lab notes and runbook content; please call out missing guardrails or suggested thresholds that are too conservative.
- We should coordinate with product for any per-customer prefetch defaults changes since this impacts long-context SLAs.

End of diary.
